messages.subject: Pooling question - a summary
parts:
Question:



> >I am unsure what is the best way to pool my data, I have line transect data

>from annual game counts over several years, with repetitions, and through

> >diverse vegetation types. Any advice would be very helpful....



> >My data set:





> >7 years (with 8-16 repetitions per year) of data of observations of 14

> >ungulate species along 8 line-transects through various amounts of 11

> >vegetation types.



> >I wish to find the long-term average density of each species per vegetation

> >type.



> >Firstly, I have analysed the data by pooling all the transects for all the

> >years and repetitions and stratifying for vegetation types. This gives me a

> >nice number of observations, to work out the density estimate per vegetation

> >type, and gives me the overall average density across the years, (which is

> >what I am interested in). However, I now realize the sample size is 1, and

> >so my variance is inaccurate - right?



> >Reply:



> >I'll ignore the species -- you can either have them all in one project file
> >with
> >a species field in the observation layer and use data selection in the data
> >filter to select each one, one by one, or you could have a separate project
> >file
> >for each species (in which case the Template option in project setup will be
> >useful to you - look up Template in the online help index).

> >Seems to me you want to try detection function pooled across all habitats,
> >separate detection functions for each habitat type and detection function as
> >a
> >covariate. We'd like to set up a project to allow you to try all 3, and get
> >valid density estimates for each case. Seems that you are not interested in
> >by-
> >year estimates, so we'll pool over years.

> >How about the following:
> >You have a stratum layer with one record for each veg type
> >You have a sample layer with one record for each transect within each veg
> >type.
> >The transect length is the length of transect in that veg type mutiplied by
> >the
> >number of times it was surveyed (e.g., surveyed 7 times in 7 years then
> >multiply
> >by 49).
> >You have an observation layer with one record for each observation. Pool
> >observations across years and repeats within years as we're not interested
> >in
> >these.

> >Then try an analysis with detection function global, another with detection
> >function by stratum and a third with the stratum label (ie veg type) as a
> >factor
> >covariate. See what AIC tells you (assuming no other problems with the
> >data),
> >but I would tend to err on the side of the higher-parameter model as you're
> >most
> >intersted in the by stratum estimates of density (ie density by habitat
> >type),
> >rather than the global density estimate; it's the latter that AIC is
> >designed to
> >give you the best bias-variance trade off on.

> >There is one problem with this analysis -- Distance thinks that the
> >transects
> >within each stratum are independent, but in fact they are not. Will only be
> >a
> >problem if you want to compare the densities among habitats to judge
> >statistical
> >significance of the difference/estimate confidence intervals on differences,
> >etc. You could do this with a bootstrap, where you bootstrap by transect
> >(ie 1-
> >8) and when you select a particular transect, the relevent parts of the
> >transect
> >are put under each habitat stratum. You'd have to program this outside of
> >Distance (calling Distance to do the analysis) -- one of these days I'll get
> >around to adding such a facility within the program (it's also useful for
> >trend
> >analysis, where you repeat transcts across years). This non-independence
> >would
> >not be a big problem if you had lots of transects, but with only 8 it may
> >cause
> >quite a covariance in estimates between veg types. Can't say without trying
> >it.



> >END
